subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In time-of-flight mass spectrometry, why must samples be ionised before detection?
options: So that the particles can be accelerated by an electric field and create a current on detection
To increase the mass of the particles
To remove the neutrons from the sample
To convert atoms into molecules
questions.explain: Ions are needed so they can be accelerated by an electric field and so that they generate a measurable current when they strike the detector.

questions.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element show a large jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies. In which group does the element lie?
options: Group 3
Group 2
Group 4
Group 1
questions.explain: A big jump after two electrons are removed shows the third electron comes from an inner, closer shell, identifying a Group 2 element.

questions.q: Which sub-shell is filled immediately after the 3p sub-shell when building up electron configurations?
options: 4d
3d
4s
4p
questions.explain: 4s is at a lower energy than 3d in the filling sequence, so 4s fills before 3d.

questions.q: Why is acidified barium chloride solution used to test for sulfate ions, and why is magnesium hydroxide used in medicine?
options: Both compounds are soluble and coloured
BaSO4 is soluble; Mg(OH)2 is a strong acid
BaSO4 forms a white precipitate as it is insoluble; Mg(OH)2 is a sparingly soluble base used as an antacid
BaSO4 is green; Mg(OH)2 is a strong oxidiser
questions.explain: The insolubility of BaSO4 gives a white precipitate confirming sulfate, while sparingly soluble Mg(OH)2 neutralises stomach acid as 'milk of magnesia'.

questions.q: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across Period 3, and the main reason?
options: It increases because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
It increases because shielding increases
It decreases because atomic radius increases
It stays constant because the shell is the same
questions.explain: First ionisation energy generally rises across Period 3 as increasing nuclear charge attracts the outer electrons more strongly with little change in shielding.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy a single atomic orbital, and why?
options: Ten, the capacity of a d sub-shell
Two, because the Pauli exclusion principle requires opposite spins
One, because of Hund's rule
Eight, to satisfy the octet rule
questions.explain: An orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins according to the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.q: What happens when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?
options: The solution turns colourless
No reaction occurs
A white precipitate of KCl forms
The solution turns orange as chlorine displaces bromine
questions.explain: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2Br- gives 2Cl- + Br2, giving an orange colour.

questions.q: Across Period 3 from Na to Ar, first ionisation energy shows a general increase but with dips at Al and S. The dip at aluminium occurs because:
options: Aluminium's outer electron is a 3p electron, higher in energy than magnesium's 3s electron
Aluminium has a full 3p sub-shell
Aluminium experiences less shielding than magnesium
Aluminium has greater nuclear charge than sulfur
questions.explain: Al's first electron is removed from a 3p orbital that lies above the filled 3s of magnesium, so less energy is needed.

questions.q: When chlorine is added to cold dilute sodium hydroxide, what type of reaction occurs and what are the products?
options: Reduction, giving only NaCl
Oxidation, giving Cl2O
Disproportionation, giving NaCl, NaClO and water
Neutralisation, giving NaClO3 only
questions.explain: Cl2 + 2NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO + H2O; chlorine is simultaneously oxidised (to +1 in ClO-) and reduced (to -1 in Cl-), so it disproportionates.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase down Group 7?
options: Hydrogen bonding increases down the group
Metallic bonding develops down the group
Molecules get larger with more electrons, so London (van der Waals) forces between molecules increase
Covalent bonds within molecules get stronger
questions.explain: Larger halogen molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: Which Cu electron configuration is correct, reflecting the stability of a full d sub-shell?
options: [Ar] 3d8 4s2
[Ar] 3d9 4s2
questions.explain: Copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 because a completely full 3d sub-shell with a single 4s electron is energetically favourable.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium, against the general trend across a period?
options: Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital of slightly higher energy than the 2s electron removed from beryllium
Beryllium's electron experiences greater shielding
Boron has fewer protons than beryllium
Boron has a half-filled 2p sub-shell that is destabilised
questions.explain: The first electron removed from boron is a 2p electron, which is at a higher energy and less tightly held than beryllium's 2s electron.

questions.q: Silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3. Why?
options: It has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure with strong Si-Si bonds throughout
It exists as Si8 molecules
It is a metal with very strong metallic bonds
It has the strongest van der Waals forces
questions.explain: Silicon forms a giant covalent lattice in which many strong Si-Si covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

questions.q: What is observed when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
options: No reaction
A yellow precipitate forms
The mixture darkens/turns brown as iodine is displaced
The solution turns colourless
questions.explain: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it displaces iodine: Br2 + 2I- gives 2Br- + I2, producing a brown solution.

questions.q: What are the products when calcium reacts with cold water?
options: Calcium hydroxide and hydrogen
Calcium oxide and hydrogen
Calcium carbonate and water
Calcium hydride and oxygen
questions.explain: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2; Group 2 metals form the hydroxide and hydrogen gas with water.

questions.q: What does the existence of successive ionisation energies that fall into distinct groups (e.g. 2, then 8, then 8) provide evidence for?
options: The arrangement of electrons in shells (energy levels)
The nuclear model of the atom
The wave nature of electrons
The existence of isotopes
questions.explain: Clusters of successive ionisation energies separated by large jumps are direct evidence that electrons occupy distinct shells.

questions.q: How many orbitals are present in a p sub-shell, and what shape are they?
options: Two orbitals, each spherical
One orbital, dumb-bell shaped
Five orbitals, each four-lobed
Three orbitals, each dumb-bell shaped
questions.explain: A p sub-shell has three dumb-bell-shaped orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles to each other.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
options: Oxygen has more shielding shells than nitrogen
In oxygen the paired 2p electrons repel, making one easier to remove than nitrogen's half-filled 2p set
Oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge
Nitrogen's 2p sub-shell is full
questions.explain: Oxygen has two electrons paired in one 2p orbital; the resulting electron-electron repulsion makes removal easier than from nitrogen's stable half-filled p sub-shell.

questions.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
options: Four-lobed (clover)
Doughnut-shaped
Dumb-bell (two lobes)
Spherical
questions.explain: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus.

questions.q: When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium iodide, why are products such as H2S and I2 formed?
options: The reaction is a simple neutralisation
Iodide ions are oxidising agents
Sulfuric acid acts only as an acid
Iodide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce sulfur from +6 to -2
questions.explain: Iodide is a powerful reducing agent and reduces sulfur in H2SO4 all the way to H2S (and gives I2), unlike chloride which only gives HCl.

questions.q: Why does sulfur (S8) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P4) in Period 3?
options: Sulfur has stronger covalent bonds within its molecules
Sulfur is a giant covalent structure
Phosphorus is metallic
S8 molecules are larger than P4 molecules, giving stronger van der Waals forces between them
questions.explain: Both are simple molecular solids, but the larger S8 molecule has more electrons and stronger London (van der Waals) forces than P4, so it melts at a higher temperature.

questions.q: After adding acidified silver nitrate, how can silver chloride be distinguished from silver iodide using ammonia?
options: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia while AgI is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia
AgCl is insoluble in all ammonia while AgI dissolves in dilute ammonia
Neither dissolves in ammonia
Both dissolve readily in dilute ammonia
questions.explain: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr dissolves only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI is insoluble in concentrated ammonia, allowing the halides to be distinguished.

questions.q: Why does sodium have a much lower melting point than aluminium in Period 3?
options: Sodium is a giant covalent structure
Aluminium delocalises three electrons per atom and has a higher charge density, giving stronger metallic bonding
Sodium has covalent bonding
Aluminium has weaker metallic bonding due to its larger ions
questions.explain: Al3+ has a smaller ion and contributes three delocalised electrons, so its metallic bonding is much stronger than that of Na, raising the melting point.

questions.q: Why does the melting point fall sharply between silicon and phosphorus in Period 3?
options: Phosphorus is a metal and silicon is not
The structure changes from giant covalent (Si) to simple molecular (P4), so only weak van der Waals forces are broken on melting phosphorus
Phosphorus has hydrogen bonding
Phosphorus has stronger covalent bonds than silicon
questions.explain: Silicon's giant covalent lattice requires breaking many strong bonds, whereas molecular P4 needs only weak London forces overcome, giving a sharp drop.

questions.q: What is the relative charge and relative mass of an electron (to the usual approximation)?
options: Charge -1, mass 1/1836
Charge -1, mass 1
Charge +1, mass 1
Charge 0, mass 1
questions.explain: An electron has a relative charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836 of a proton.

questions.q: Which statement about the 4s and 3d sub-shells is correct?
options: 3d fills first and empties first
4s fills first but 4s empties first on ionisation
4s fills first and 3d empties first on ionisation
3d fills first but 4s empties first
questions.explain: 4s fills before 3d during the build-up, yet 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons when the atom is ionised.

questions.q: Which best explains the general decrease in atomic radius across Period 3 from Na to Ar?
options: Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell of electrons closer; shielding stays roughly constant
Electrons are added to new shells, increasing the radius
The number of neutrons decreases across the period
Shielding increases faster than nuclear charge
questions.explain: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding, so the outer electrons are pulled in and the radius decreases.

questions.q: During electron impact ionisation in a mass spectrometer, what happens to the sample particles?
options: They are accelerated without any charge change
They gain an electron to form negative ions
A high-energy electron knocks out an electron, forming a 1+ positive ion
They are split into protons and neutrons
questions.explain: A high-energy electron from an electron gun knocks an electron off each particle, typically forming 1+ ions.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of a molecule, which peak corresponds to the molecular ion?
options: The peak at m/z = 1
The peak at the lowest m/z value
The peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring isotope peaks), equal to the relative molecular mass
The most intense (base) peak
questions.explain: The molecular ion peak is the one at the highest m/z (the M peak), and its value equals the relative molecular mass.

questions.q: Why is barium more reactive than calcium toward water?
options: Barium has a higher first ionisation energy so reacts faster
Barium has fewer protons than calcium
Barium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily, making it more reactive
Calcium has a larger atomic radius than barium
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are further out and more shielded, lowering ionisation energy, so barium loses electrons (and reacts) more readily than calcium.
